questions.question_text: Find the component of $\underset{\sim}{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$ perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

options.why: Gave the parallel component (the projection) instead of the perpendicular one.
Computed $\text{proj}_{\underset{\sim}{b}}\underset{\sim}{a}-\underset{\sim}{a}$ instead of $\underset{\sim}{a}-\text{proj}_{\underset{\sim}{b}}\underset{\sim}{a}$.
Subtracted the component products, $(2)(1)-(7)(3) = -19$, when finding the dot product.

questions.question_text: Resolve $\underset{\sim}{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$ into a component parallel to $\underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and a component perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{b}$. Which pair gives the parallel component first, then the perpendicular component?

options.why: Named the two components the wrong way round; the parallel component is the multiple of $\underset{\sim}{b}$.
Subtracted $\underset{\sim}{a}$ from the projection instead of the projection from $\underset{\sim}{a}$.
Used $|\underset{\sim}{b}|^{2} = 3^2 = 9$, leaving the $y$-component out of the magnitude.

questions.question_text: A student resolves $\underset{\sim}{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ relative to $\underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and writes the parallel component as $\underset{\sim}{p} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ and the perpendicular component as $\underset{\sim}{q} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Which statement about this decomposition is correct?

options.why: Ran only the addition check and skipped the perpendicularity check, which the decomposition fails.
The addition check does hold: $(2,4)+(4,1) = (6,5) = \underset{\sim}{a}$.

options.text: It is wrong, because $\underset{\sim}{p}$ is not parallel to $\underset{\sim}{b}$.
options.why: $(2,4) = 2(1,2)$ is parallel to $\underset{\sim}{b}$; the failure is in the perpendicularity of $\underset{\sim}{q}$.

questions.solution_text:
Check 1: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$, so the components do add back to $\underset{\sim}{a}$.
Check 2: $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = 4+2 = 6$
Since this is not $0$, $\underset{\sim}{q}$ is not perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{b}$ and the decomposition is wrong.

questions.question_text: Find the component of $\underset{\sim}{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

options.why: Gave the parallel component (the projection) instead of the perpendicular one.
Subtracted $\underset{\sim}{a}$ from the projection instead of the projection from $\underset{\sim}{a}$.
Left the $z$-terms out of the dot product, using $5+1 = 6$ instead of $9$.

questions.question_text: Find the magnitude of the component of $\underset{\sim}{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$ perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

options.why: Gave the length of the parallel component (the scalar projection) instead of the perpendicular one.
Gave $|\underset{\sim}{a}|$, the length of the whole vector, rather than of its perpendicular component.
Stopped at the scalar $\frac{29}{25}$ without multiplying by the length $5$ of $\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question_text: The points $A(3,2)$ and $B(-1,10)$ are given. Find the component of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{c} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

options.why: Gave the parallel component (the projection) instead of the perpendicular one.
Subtracted $\overrightarrow{AB}$ from the projection instead of the projection from $\overrightarrow{AB}$.
Used the dot product $4$ as the scalar without dividing by $|\underset{\sim}{c}|^{2} = 2$.

questions.question_text: The angle between $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$ is $120^{\circ}$ and $|\underset{\sim}{a}| = 20$. Find the exact magnitude of the component of $\underset{\sim}{a}$ perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{b}$.

options.why: Used $|\underset{\sim}{a}|\cos 120^{\circ}$, which gives the parallel component's magnitude, not the perpendicular one.
Treated the obtuse angle as making the answer negative; a magnitude is never negative.
Used $\sin 120^{\circ} = \sqrt{3}$ instead of $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

questions.question_text: A vector $\underset{\sim}{a}$ has component $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ parallel to $\underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and component $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{b}$. Find $\underset{\sim}{a}$.

options.why: Subtracted the parallel component from the perpendicular one instead of adding the two components.
Subtracted the perpendicular component from the parallel one instead of adding the two components.
Added $\underset{\sim}{b}$ to the perpendicular component instead of adding the parallel component.

questions.solution_text:
The two components add back to give the original vector.
$\underset{\sim}{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$
$= \begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$
Check: $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = 6-6 = 0$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} = 2\underset{\sim}{b}$
